then.text: Come back any time. The Hoard isn't going anywhere, which is rather the point of a museum.
You found our detectorist? Wonderful. Then a quick question, to make sure it all went in.
What was most of the Staffordshire Hoard?
Exactly right! Fittings stripped from swords and helmets: war gear, made by the finest craftsmen of the 600s and 700s. Why it was buried, nobody knows.
Take this. A garnet, set in gold the way the Saxon smiths did it, over a little piece of patterned gold foil so it sparkles. A replica, before you ask.

else.text: Not quite. Have another look at the cases with the Gallery Guide, and think about what a warrior would carry.

then.text: Now go and find out how it was found. There's a detectorist who sweeps the fields below the Roaches. He knows the story backwards.

else.text: Start with the cases. The Gallery Guide by the Hoard will talk you through them.
Welcome to the Potteries Museum! We've the finest collection of Staffordshire ceramics in the world, a Spitfire, and the Staffordshire Hoard.
Thousands of pieces of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver, found in a field in 2009. Would you like to really understand it? Then let's make a little project of it.
Look at the cases with the Gallery Guide, then find out how it was found. When you're done, I'll ask you one question.

then.text: Don't forget to look at the folded cross. Somebody bent it on purpose before it was buried.
Right, the cases. Look at all these little gold fittings with red garnets: they're from the hilts of swords. There are dozens of them.
Garnets came from as far away as India and Sri Lanka. Each one was cut to shape by hand and set over gold foil to catch the light.
There's a helmet, pieced back together from hundreds of fragments, and a strip of gold with a Latin prayer asking God to scatter the enemy. Bit of a theme, really.

else.text: Mind the glass, it's been polished. By me. Twice.

then.text: Lovely oatcake, that. I'll be guarding the Spitfire with renewed vigour.
An oatcake, plain with butter? Oh, you are an angel. Not in front of the exhibits, mind. Crumbs.
The Spitfire's a Mark 16, built near the end of the war. Kids always ask if it still flies. I tell them only on Tuesdays.

else.text: No flash photography of the Hoard, please. It's been in the dark for thirteen hundred years. It gets headaches.

museum_kid.text: Miss says the Hoard's worth millions but we're not allowed to touch it. What's the point of gold you can't touch?
